[S:e74059ccc6ab#49] [S:bb5f6c31dd84#52] [S:bb5f6c31dd84#55]

- **1706.03762v7.pdf, page 8, Table 2:** “Transformer (base model) 27.3 38.1 3.3 · 1018 Transformer (big) 28.4 41.8 2.3 · 1019”; the table labels its BLEU columns “EN-DE EN-FR,” supporting English-to-German scores of **27.3** and **28.4**, respectively. [S:e74059ccc6ab#49]
- **1705.03122v3.pdf, page 6, Table 1:** “ConvS2S (BPE 40K) 25.16” appears under “WMT’14 English-German,” and its caption states, “ConvS2S and GNMT results are averaged over several runs.” [S:bb5f6c31dd84#52] **Page 5** specifies: “We report average results over three runs of each model, where each differs only in the initial random seed.” [S:bb5f6c31dd84#44]

The Transformer paper also lists the single-model ConvS2S English-to-German result as **25.16**, agreeing with the ConvS2S paper’s mean result. [S:e74059ccc6ab#49] [S:bb5f6c31dd84#52] The ensemble entries differ—**26.43** in the ConvS2S paper versus **26.36** in the Transformer paper—and the supplied evidence does not explain that discrepancy. answer:
Verdict: SUPPORTED

Evidence for:
- The randomized trial used a 24-week home-based physical activity program and an education/usual-care control group; 170 participants were randomized (1642727.pdf, p.1: “A total of 170 participants were randomized”; “Participants were randomly allocated to an education and usual care group or to a 24-week home-based program of physical activity.”). [S:d8d7acaab8e3#1]
- Cognitive assessors were blinded (1642727.pdf, p.1: “Assessors of cognitive function were blinded to group membership.”). [S:d8d7acaab8e3#0]
- At intervention completion, ADAS-Cog improved by 0.26 points from baseline in the activity group, while usual care deteriorated by 1.04 points (1642727.pdf, p.1: “participants in the intervention group improved 0.26 points”; “those in the usual care group deteriorated 1.04 points”). [S:d8d7acaab8e3#1]
- The between-group difference favored physical activity, with a confidence interval excluding zero (1642727.pdf, p.1: “The absolute difference of the outcome measure between the intervention and control groups was -1.3 points (95% confidence interval,-2.38 to -0.22) at the end of the intervention.”). [S:d8d7acaab8e3#2]
- The authors explicitly concluded that six months provided a modest cognitive benefit (1642727.pdf, p.1: “In this study of adults with subjective memory impairment, a 6-month program of physical activity provided a modest improvement in cognition over an 18-month follow-up period.”). [S:d8d7acaab8e3#3]

Evidence against and qualifications:
- Improvement varied by cognitive outcome: delayed recall and Clinical Dementia Rating improved modestly, but immediate recall, digit symbol coding, and verbal fluency did not change significantly (1642727.pdf, p.1: “Word list delayed recall and Clinical Dementia Rating sum of boxes improved modestly as well, whereas word list total immediate recall, digit symbol coding, verbal fluency, Beck depression score, and Medical Outcomes 36-Item Short-Form physical and mental component summaries did not change significantly.”). [S:d8d7acaab8e3#3]
- The activity group's improvement from baseline alone was uncertain because its confidence interval included zero (1642727.pdf, p.1: “participants in the intervention group improved 0.26 points (95% confidence interval, -0.89 to 0.54)”). [S:d8d7acaab8e3#1]
- Follow-up was incomplete (1642727.pdf, p.1: “A total of 170 participants were randomized and 138 participants completed the 18-month assessment.”). [S:d8d7acaab8e3#1]
- Support is specific to participants with memory complaints without dementia (1642727.pdf, p.1: “We recruited volunteers who reported memory problems but did not meet criteria for dementia.”). [S:d8d7acaab8e3#0]

The supplied abstract does not provide a detailed limitations discussion or establish whether the benefit generalizes to other populations.

answer:
Verdict: SUPPORTED

Evidence for:
- The support is specific to depression: bariatric surgery was consistently associated with lower postoperative depression prevalence across 7 studies (8%–74% decreases) and lower depressive symptom severity across 6 studies (40%–70% decreases). [S:486beda60ab3#3]
- The paper characterizes the evidence linking surgery to lower postoperative depression rates as moderate quality. [S:486beda60ab3#3]

Evidence against and limits:
- The supplied findings establish an association with improved depression outcomes; they do not establish that surgery causes improvements across mental health generally. [S:486beda60ab3#3]
- Depression and binge eating disorder were assessed before surgery, but the supplied postoperative mental health results concern depression prevalence and depressive symptom severity. [S:486beda60ab3#2] [S:486beda60ab3#3]

The paper is a meta-analysis, and its methods include risk-of-bias assessment and GRADE evidence ratings. [S:486beda60ab3#0] [S:486beda60ab3#1] The supplied passages do not specify follow-up duration, individual study designs, or detailed limitations, so they are insufficient to assess causal attribution fully.

answer:
Verdict: NOT ENOUGH EVIDENCE

Evidence for:
- The paper measures appearance as perceived age from photographs and uses leucocyte telomere length as a molecular ageing biomarker (14079881.pdf, p. 1: “perceived age of twins from photographs”; “molecular biomarker of ageing (leucocyte telomere length)”). [S:91c861203da3#0]
- It directly reports an association after controlling for chronological age and sex (14079881.pdf, p. 1: “Perceived age, controlled for chronological age and sex, also correlated significantly with physical and cognitive functioning as well as with leucocyte telomere length.”). [S:91c861203da3#1]

Evidence against concluding a close link:
- The reported correlation establishes statistical significance, but the supplied passage gives neither its direction nor its magnitude, so it cannot establish that greater cellular ageing closely links to an older appearance (14079881.pdf, p. 1: “correlated significantly with … leucocyte telomere length”). [S:91c861203da3#1]
- The study is a follow-up study in a Danish twin cohort comprising 1826 twins aged at least 70, limiting the population directly represented by this evidence (14079881.pdf, p. 1: “DESIGN Follow-up study”; “Population based twin cohort in Denmark”; “1826 twins aged >or=70”). [S:91c861203da3#0]

answer:
Verdict: SUPPORTED

Evidence for:
- The trial studied thigh-length GCS in 2,518 immobile patients hospitalized within one week of acute stroke (11718220.pdf, p. 1: “2518 patients who were admitted to hospital within 1 week of an acute stroke and who were immobile”). [S:75ce2242eb8a#0]
- Symptomatic or asymptomatic popliteal or femoral DVT occurred in 126 (10.0%) patients assigned stockings versus 133 (10.5%) controls; the reduction was not statistically significant (11718220.pdf, p. 1: “a non-significant absolute reduction in risk of 0.5% (95% CI -1.9% to 2.9%)”). [S:75ce2242eb8a#1]
- The authors concluded against their use (11718220.pdf, p. 1: “These data do not lend support to the use of thigh-length GCS in patients admitted to hospital with acute stroke.”). [S:75ce2242eb8a#2]

Evidence against / qualification:
- The numerical difference favored stockings, but the confidence interval included zero; the evidence supports no demonstrated reduction rather than proof of exactly no effect (11718220.pdf, p. 1: “a non-significant absolute reduction in risk of 0.5% (95% CI -1.9% to 2.9%)”). [S:75ce2242eb8a#1]

Evidence against the claim:
- The paper explicitly concludes that somatic sexual differentiation is substantially cell autonomous: “Our study demonstrates that avian somatic cells possess an inherent sex identity and that, in birds, sexual differentiation is substantively cell autonomous.” (4388470.pdf, p. 1.) [S:c49276a0ec82#1]
- The researchers transplanted presumptive mesoderm between chicken embryos of opposite sexes; “in chicken mixed-sex chimaeras the donor cells were excluded from the functional structures of the host gonad.” (4388470.pdf, p. 1.) [S:c49276a0ec82#1]
- Female donor cells in a developing testis retained their sexual identity: “donor cells contributing to the developing testis retained a female identity and expressed a marker of female function.” (4388470.pdf, p. 1.) [S:c49276a0ec82#1]
- Observations of three lateral gynandromorph chickens also supported intrinsic cellular sex identity: “These studies demonstrated that gynandromorph birds are genuine male:female chimaeras, and indicated that male and female avian somatic cells may have an inherent sex identity.” (4388470.pdf, p. 1.) [S:c49276a0ec82#0]

Evidence for the claim: None in the supplied passages; the reported conclusion states that sexual differentiation is “substantively cell autonomous.” (4388470.pdf, p. 1.) [S:c49276a0ec82#1]

Limitations: The supplied evidence identifies chickens and presumptive mesoderm contributing to gonads, but does not name specific somatic cell subtypes or the female-function marker; its conclusion concerns substantive cell autonomy in sexual differentiation. (4388470.pdf, p. 1: “we transplanted presumptive mesoderm”; “expressed a marker of female function”; “sexual differentiation is substantively cell autonomous.”) [S:c49276a0ec82#1]

Evidence for: No supplied passage supports higher methylation age.

Evidence against: Caloric restriction was associated with younger blood methylation age in rhesus monkeys: “Twenty-two to 30-year-old rhesus monkeys exposed to 30% caloric restriction since 7-14 years of age showed attenuation of age-related methylation drift compared to ad libitum-fed controls such that their blood methylation age appeared 7 years younger than their chronologic age.” (22038539.pdf, p. 1.) The seven-year difference compares methylation age with chronological age; the comparison with controls concerns attenuation of methylation drift. [S:d8840874b2eb#0]

A second complete passage states: “Here, the authors provide evidence that age-related methylation drift correlates with lifespan and that caloric restriction in mice and rhesus monkeys results in attenuation of age-related methylation drift.” (22038539.pdf, p. 1.) [S:d8840874b2eb#1]

Interpretation limits: The supplied evidence names caloric restriction but does not explicitly define the abbreviation CR. It provides no methylation-age measurement method, clock specification, uncertainty estimates, or methodological limitations. The verdict therefore applies to caloric restriction, conditional on that being the intended meaning of CR.

answer:
Verdict: REFUTED

Evidence for: No supplied passage supports increased lung fibrosis or directly establishes an effect on lung inflammation.

Evidence against:
- Pharmacological AMPK activation decreases fibrotic activity in human IPF lung myofibroblasts, enhances mitochondrial biogenesis, and normalizes sensitivity to apoptosis. [S:6316519c6ccf#1] In 49556906.pdf, p.1: “Pharmacological activation of AMPK in myofibroblasts from lungs of humans with IPF display lower fibrotic activity, along with enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis and normalization of sensitivity to apoptosis.”
- Metformin accelerates resolution of established fibrosis in bleomycin-treated mice in an AMPK-dependent manner, supporting a causal role for AMPK in the reported antifibrotic effect. [S:6316519c6ccf#1] In 49556906.pdf, p.1: “In a bleomycin model of lung fibrosis in mice, metformin therapeutically accelerates the resolution of well-established fibrosis in an AMPK-dependent manner.”
- Human IPF lungs and an experimental mouse model show lower AMPK activity in fibrotic regions associated with apoptosis-resistant myofibroblasts. [S:6316519c6ccf#0] In 49556906.pdf, p.1: “AMPK activity is lower in fibrotic regions associated with metabolically active and apoptosis-resistant myofibroblasts.”

The supplied evidence contradicts the proposed direction of the fibrosis effect, but does not report direct inflammatory outcomes, specific inflammation-related signaling pathways, or the experimental controls establishing AMPK dependence.

answer:
Verdict: REFUTED

Evidence for: No supplied passage supports decreased thrombosis rates; the reported association is higher fibrinogen with graft occlusion. [S:70cf99c0017a#1]

Evidence against:
- Plasma fibrinogen concentrations were significantly higher in patients with occluded grafts (p less than 0.001). [S:70cf99c0017a#1] In 12991445.pdf, page 1, the verbatim passage reports: “plasma concentrations of fibrinogen (p less than 0.001) and apolipoproteins AI (p less than 0.04) and (a) (p less than 0.05) were significantly higher in patients with occluded grafts.” [S:70cf99c0017a#1]
- Graft patency was 90% below the median fibrinogen concentration versus 57% above it, supporting an association with increased occlusion rather than decreased occlusion. [S:70cf99c0017a#2] In 12991445.pdf, page 1: “Patency was significantly higher by life table analysis in patients with a plasma fibrinogen concentration below the median than in those with a concentration above (90% v 57%, p less than 0.0002).” [S:70cf99c0017a#2]

Limitations: The supplied evidence concerns one-year patency of saphenous vein femoropopliteal bypass grafts in a prospective study of 157 patients. [S:70cf99c0017a#0] In 12991445.pdf, page 1: “MAIN OUTCOME MEASURE Cumulative percentage patency at one year.” [S:70cf99c0017a#0] The fibrinogen comparison uses concentrations above versus below the median, without specifying a hyperfibrinogenemia threshold or separately reporting thrombosis-specific rates in that passage. [S:70cf99c0017a#2]

Evidence for: The paper reports that each 5 kg/m² higher BMI above the stated reference range was associated with about 30% higher overall mortality; this finding concerns mortality, not quality of life (195689316.pdf, p. 1: “each 5 kg/m(2) higher BMI was on average associated with about 30% higher overall mortality”). [S:01f6619dc17e#3]

Evidence against: No supplied passage directly contradicts the claim; the study assessed baseline BMI versus mortality, so its reported outcome does not answer whether obesity lowers quality of life (195689316.pdf, p. 1: “Collaborative analyses were undertaken of baseline BMI versus mortality in 57 prospective studies”). [S:01f6619dc17e#1]

Causation and limitations: The authors describe excess mortality above the reference range as “probably largely causal,” but that interpretation concerns mortality and does not establish a causal effect on quality of life (195689316.pdf, p. 1: “The progressive excess mortality above this range is due mainly to vascular disease and is probably largely causal.”). [S:01f6619dc17e#4] They excluded the first five years of follow-up to limit reverse causality (195689316.pdf, p. 1: “To limit reverse causality, the first 5 years of follow-up were excluded”). [S:01f6619dc17e#2]

answer:
The paper explicitly claims state-of-the-art KBQA accuracy on **SimpleQuestions** and **WebQSP**, with an important qualification: its detailed results describe a new best result on SimpleQuestions and a result comparable to the state of the art on WebQSP. [S:b52dd916fadb#1] [S:b52dd916fadb#74]

- **SimpleQuestions (single-relation QA):** The multiple-detector system achieves **78.7% test accuracy**, compared with **76.4%** for AMPCNN; the single-detector system achieves **77.0%** (1704.06194.pdf, p.9, Table 3: “Our Method 77.0 63.0” and “Our Method (multi-detectors) 78.7 63.9”). [S:b52dd916fadb#73] The authors explicitly describe the multiple-detector result as “a new state-of-the-art result on SimpleQuestions” (1704.06194.pdf, p.9). [S:b52dd916fadb#74]
- **WebQSP (multi-relation QA):** The multiple-detector system achieves **63.9% test accuracy**, matching STAGG’s **63.9%**; the single-detector system achieves **63.0%** (1704.06194.pdf, p.9, Table 3: “STAGG 72.8 63.9” and “Our Method (multi-detectors) 78.7 63.9”). [S:b52dd916fadb#73] The authors qualify this as “a result comparable to the state-of-the-art on WebQSP” (1704.06194.pdf, p.9). [S:b52dd916fadb#74]

For the separate **relation detection tasks**, HR-BiLSTM achieves **93.3% accuracy on SimpleQuestions** and **82.53% on WebQSP**, the highest scores listed in Table 2 (1704.06194.pdf, p.8: “Hier-Res-BiLSTM (HR-BiLSTM) words + rel names 93.3 82.53”). [S:b52dd916fadb#62]

citations.claim: The abstract claims state-of-the-art KBQA accuracy on the single-relation SimpleQuestions and multi-relation WebQSP benchmarks.
citations.quote:
Relation detection is a core component of
many NLP applications including Knowl-
edge Base Question Answering (KBQA).
In this paper, we propose a hierarchi-
cal recurrent neural network enhanced by
residual learning which detects KB re-
lations given an input question.
Our
method uses deep residual bidirectional
LSTMs to compare questions and rela-
tion names via different levels of abstrac-
tion.
Additionally, we propose a sim-
ple KBQA system that integrates entity
linking and our proposed relation detec-
tor to make the two components enhance
each other. Our experimental results show
that our approach not only achieves out-
standing relation detection performance,
but more importantly, it helps our KBQA
system achieve state-of-the-art accuracy
for both single-relation (SimpleQuestions)
and multi-relation (WebQSP) QA bench-
marks.

answer:
The paper proposes **Hierarchical Residual BiLSTM (HR-BiLSTM)** for detecting knowledge-base relations from an input question. It uses a hierarchical recurrent neural network enhanced with residual learning. [S:dbedd9145a18#39] [S:dbedd9145a18#1]

The framework uses:

- **Two relation representations:** relation-level representations treat each complete relation name as one token; word-level representations treat the tokenized relation name as a sequence of words. [S:dbedd9145a18#27] [S:dbedd9145a18#28]
- **Deep bidirectional LSTMs:** these learn question representations at different abstraction levels to match different levels of relation information. [S:dbedd9145a18#15]
- **Hierarchical matching:** the input question is matched against both word-level and relation-level representations of each candidate relation. [S:dbedd9145a18#30]
- **Residual learning and shortcut connections:** residual learning makes training easier and supports deeper question representations; shortcut connections enable hierarchical matching between question layers and relations. [S:dbedd9145a18#15] [S:dbedd9145a18#39]

The authors also integrate the relation detector with **entity linking in a KBQA system**, allowing the two components to enhance each other. [S:dbedd9145a18#1] The detector first re-ranks candidate entities using their connections to confidently detected relations, then finds core relations or relation chains for the remaining topic-entity candidates. [S:dbedd9145a18#16] Queries use the detected entity and relation to retrieve answers from the knowledge base. [S:dbedd9145a18#14] For questions requiring additional constraints, an optional constraint-detection step uses text matching and entity linking over a generated KB subgraph. [S:dbedd9145a18#16] [S:dbedd9145a18#54]

1708.01464.pdf reports three evaluation metrics:

- **Phoneme Error Rate (PER):** Levenshtein distance between predicted and gold-standard phoneme sequences, divided by the gold-standard sequence length. [S:f53854feabef#26]
- **Word Error Rate (WER):** Percentage of words whose predicted phoneme sequence does not exactly match the gold-standard sequence. [S:f53854feabef#26]
- **Word Error Rate 100 (WER 100):** Percentage of test words for which the correct pronunciation is absent from the system’s first 100 guesses. [S:f53854feabef#27]

For evaluations covering multiple languages, each metric is averaged with equal weight per language. [S:f53854feabef#27]

Verbatim supporting passages from **1708.01464.pdf, page 4**:

> “We use the following three evaluation metrics:” and “Phoneme Error Rate (PER) is the Lev- enshtein distance between the predicted phoneme sequences and the gold standard phoneme sequences, divided by the length of the gold standard phoneme sequences.” [S:f53854feabef#26]

> “Word Error Rate (WER) is the percentage of words in which the predicted phoneme se- quence does not exactly match the gold stan- dard phoneme sequence.” [S:f53854feabef#26]

> “Word Error Rate 100 (WER 100) is the per- centage of words in the test set for which the correct guess is not in the ﬁrst 100 guesses of the system.” [S:f53854feabef#27]

> “In system evaluations, WER, WER 100, and PER numbers presented for multiple languages are averaged, weighting each language equally (fol- lowing Deri and Knight, 2016).” [S:f53854feabef#27]

Its reported results in 1801.05147.pdf (p. 6) are:

| Dataset | Precision | Recall | F1 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| DL-PS | 89.56% | 82.70% | **85.99%** |
| EC-MT | 76.33% | 74.00% | **75.15%** |
| EC-UQ | 74.72% | 68.60% | **71.53%** |

The DL-PS results appear in Table 2: “ALCrowd 89.56 82.70 85.99”. [S:7eeec5ab25a7#55] The EC results appear in Table 3: “ALCrowd 76.33 74.00 75.15” for EC-MT and “ALCrowd 74.72 68.60 71.53” for EC-UQ. [S:7eeec5ab25a7#56]

DL-PS contains chatbot dialog sentences with person-name and song-name entities. [S:7eeec5ab25a7#46] EC-MT contains merchandise titles, and EC-UQ contains user queries, with brand, product, model, material, and specification entities. [S:7eeec5ab25a7#48]

answer:
The paper introduces a paragraph-level neural network that models dependencies between discourse units and predicts a sequence of discourse relations within a paragraph. [S:3d8f1f45f0ef#0] Evaluation uses PDTB v2.0 and its four top-level classes—Comparison, Contingency, Expansion and Temporal—with sections 2–20 for training, 21–22 for testing and 0–1 for development. [S:3d8f1f45f0ef#31]

For **four-way implicit relation classification**, the full model achieves **48.82 macro-F1 versus the previous best 47.80**, an absolute improvement of **1.02 points**, or approximately **2.13% relative**; its accuracy is 57.44%, while the highest previous accuracy listed is 57.57%, so this variant does not improve accuracy. [S:3d8f1f45f0ef#45] The untied-parameter variant achieves 58.20% accuracy, improving that previous accuracy by 0.63 percentage points. [S:3d8f1f45f0ef#45]

The ten-run majority-vote ensemble reaches 51.84 implicit macro-F1, adding 3.02 points over the full single model. [S:3d8f1f45f0ef#58] The highest ensemble accuracy is 59.85%, achieved by the untied-parameter variant; the CRF ensemble achieves 59.75% accuracy. [S:3d8f1f45f0ef#52]

For **binary implicit relation classification**, the untied-parameter model improves Comparison F1 from the best listed previous 40.87 to 46.79 (**+5.92 points**) and Temporal from 38.84 to 45.61 (**+6.77 points**), but falls below previous best scores on Contingency (57.09 versus 58.96) and Expansion (70.41 versus 72.47). [S:3d8f1f45f0ef#51]

The comparison has important conditions: single-model results average ten runs, whereas many previous works reported their best performance. [S:3d8f1f45f0ef#42] The full model jointly predicts implicit and explicit relations with equal loss weights. [S:3d8f1f45f0ef#27] The CRF layer is unsuitable for binary classification, so the binary gains use the untied-parameter model. [S:3d8f1f45f0ef#57]

citations.claim: The paper introduces a paragraph-level neural network that models discourse-unit dependencies and predicts sequences of discourse relations.
citations.quote:
Improving Implicit Discourse Relation Classiﬁcation by Modeling
Inter-dependencies of Discourse Units in a Paragraph
Zeyu Dai, Ruihong Huang
Department of Computer Science and Engineering
Texas A&M University
{jzdaizeyu, huangrh}@tamu.edu
Abstract
We argue that semantic meanings of a sentence
or clause can not be interpreted independently
from the rest of a paragraph, or independently
from all discourse relations and the overall
paragraph-level discourse structure. With the
goal of improving implicit discourse relation
classiﬁcation, we introduce a paragraph-level
neural networks that model inter-dependencies
between discourse units as well as discourse
relation continuity and patterns, and predict a
sequence of discourse relations in a paragraph.
Experimental results show that our model out-
performs the previous state-of-the-art systems
on the benchmark corpus of PDTB.

The paper evaluated three NER models: Stanford NER, spaCy 2.0, and a recurrent BiLSTM–CRF model (1810.08699.pdf, p. 4: “We trained and evaluated Stanford NER4, spaCy 2.05, and a recurrent model”). [S:f9433063fc7f#32]

- **Stanford NER:** a CRF classifier using lexical and contextual features (p. 4: “Stanford NER is conditional random ﬁelds (CRF) classiﬁer based on lexical and contextual features”). [S:f9433063fc7f#33]
- **spaCy 2.0:** a CNN-based transition system with Bloom embeddings and residual CNNs (p. 4: “spaCy 2.0 uses a CNN-based transition system for named entity recognition”; “a Bloom embedding is calculated”; “using residual CNNs”). [S:f9433063fc7f#33]
- **Recurrent BiLSTM–CRF:** character representations are concatenated with distributional word vectors, processed by a second BiLSTM, and labeled by a CRF (p. 4: “This representation gets concatenated with a distributional word vector such as GloVe”; “Using another bidirectional LSTM cell”; “Finally, a CRF layer labels the sequence”). [S:f9433063fc7f#37] The experiments used Genthial’s implementation, with character BiLSTM size 100 and second BiLSTM size 300 (p. 4: “We set the size of character-based biLSTM to 100 and the size of second biLSTM network to 300.”). [S:f9433063fc7f#38]

For the recurrent model, the best reported configuration used batch size 8 and Adam with initial learning rate 0.001; 50-dimensional GloVe vectors performed best among the four sizes tested (1810.08699.pdf, p. 5: “a batch size of 8 and Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 0.001”; “vectors of size 50 producing the best results”). [S:f9433063fc7f#43] spaCy was tested with the same embedding sizes—50, 100, 200, and 300—and performed best with 200 dimensions (p. 5: “GloVe word vector models of four different sizes (50, 100, 200, and 300) were tested”; “For spaCy 2.0 named entity recognizer, the same word embedding models were tested”; “the performance of 200-dimensional embeddings was highest”). [S:f9433063fc7f#43]

answer:
The experiments use two named corpora:

- **IITB English–Hindi parallel corpus:** 1.46 million training sentences and a 520-sentence development set. In 1811.00383.pdf, p. 3, the dataset passage states: “(1.46M sentences from the training set)” and “We use the 520-sentence dev-set of the IITB”. [S:30465a1b9395#15]
- **ILCI (Indian Language Corpora Initiative) parallel corpus:** 44.7K English–Hindi sentences for training; the multilingual corpus covers health and tourism. In 1811.00383.pdf, p. 3: “the ILCI English-Hindi parallel corpus (44.7K sentences)” and “spans multiple Indian languages from the health and tourism domains.” [S:30465a1b9395#15]
- **Child-task evaluation:** 2,000 ILCI sentences per task. In 1811.00383.pdf, p. 3: “For each child task, we use 2K sentences from ILCI corpus as test set.” [S:30465a1b9395#16] The child tasks translate Bengali, Gujarati, Marathi, Malayalam and Tamil into Hindi. [S:30465a1b9395#15]

The supplied passages also describe experiments with child-task parallel training data, but do not explicitly name its corpus source. [S:30465a1b9395#28]

They calculate a static embedding **separately for each word and each chosen layer**, taking the first principal component of that word’s contextualized representations: “we can create static embeddings for each word by taking the ﬁrst principal component (PC) of its contextualized representations in a given layer” (1909.00512.pdf, p. 8). [S:ac9c37278261#53]

The reported embeddings use ELMo layers 1–2 and BERT/GPT-2 layers 1, 2, 11, and 12; the table specifies that each embedding is the first principal component from a given layer (1909.00512.pdf, p. 8: “For the contextualizing models (ELMo, BERT, GPT-2), we use the ﬁrst principal component of a word’s contextualized representations in a given layer as its static embedding.”). [S:ac9c37278261#52]

For input sentences, the paper identifies the SemEval Semantic Textual Similarity datasets: “Our input data come from the SemEval Semantic Textual Similarity tasks from years 2012 - 2016” (1909.00512.pdf, p. 3). [S:ac9c37278261#18]

The supplied evidence does not specify how many occurrences are collected per word for constructing these embeddings, how those occurrences are sampled, how subword tokens are combined, or whether the vectors are centered or normalized before extracting the first principal component. The explicit 1K sampling statement concerns contextuality measures and their baselines: “both the raw measure and baseline are estimated with 1K uniformly randomly sampled word representations” (1909.00512.pdf, p. 4). [S:ac9c37278261#28] Consequently, that statement alone does not establish a 1K-occurrence recipe for each static embedding.

answer:
In **1909.09067.pdf**, the corpus includes **font type and font style**, explicitly including italics and bold print, stored as attributes of individual tokens; token positions on the physical page are recorded for PDFs only. [S:010beb8d6434#34]

A separate **fonts layer** preserves detailed font configurations referenced by the tokens. [S:010beb8d6434#35] Figure 2 illustrates tokens with `font="F0"` and a corresponding font entry containing the name `TradeGothic-BoldTwo`, full name, font format (`Type 1 CFF`), embedding status, ascender, cap height, italic angle, descender, weight, and x-height. [S:010beb8d6434#41]

Related text formatting includes paragraph and line segmentation, represented through `textspan` elements in the `textstructure` layer, plus physical page segmentation for PDFs only. [S:010beb8d6434#34] During HTML processing, paragraph/line structure and typography such as boldface and italics were retained; PDF processing used PDFlib TET to extract text and record structure, typography, and images in TETML XML. [S:010beb8d6434#22]

The representation required extending TCF because it did not readily accommodate all the annotation types. [S:010beb8d6434#34] As an application, the paper reports that features including counts of words in a particular font type and adherence to a one-sentence-per-line rule were predictive of simplified German text difficulty, although detailed results are outside the paper’s scope. [S:010beb8d6434#38]

The supplied evidence does not establish whether font size, text colour, or underlining are recorded, or whether typography preservation is complete across documents.

answer:
The paper’s main abstractive summarization model is **PG-net**, described as pointer networks with a coverage mechanism from See, Liu, and Manning (2017). The authors apply domain transfer by pretraining it on CNN/DM and then fine-tuning it on student reflections. [S:b0f720bd7a6a#17]

The underlying approach uses an encoder–decoder with attention, pointer networks to address out-of-vocabulary words, and a coverage mechanism to address word repetition. [S:b0f720bd7a6a#8]

**Fast-RL**—fast abstractive summarization with reinforcement learning from Chen and Bansal (2018)—is an additional model the authors tested. It showed similar behavior to PG-net but lower performance, so the paper reports only PG-net experiments because of space limitations. [S:b0f720bd7a6a#18] The paper also compares against the extractive component of Fast-RL as a baseline. [S:b0f720bd7a6a#32]

1706.03762v7.pdf decodes with beam width 4 and length penalty α = 0.6, whereas 1705.03122v3.pdf uses beam width 5 and length normalization by |y|^α with α tuned on newstest2015; consequently, their published BLEU gap alone does not isolate the architectural effect because decoding settings also differ. [S:bee0d5905ca6#53] [S:f74f0352f640#44]

- **1706.03762v7.pdf, p.8:** “We used beam search with a beam size of 4 and length penalty α = 0.6 [38].” The paper adds: “These hyperparameters were chosen after experimentation on the development set.” The supplied passage does not specify the penalty’s formula. [S:bee0d5905ca6#53]
- **1705.03122v3.pdf, p.5:** “We use a beam of width 5.” Its general description divides final-hypothesis log-likelihoods by length, while its WMT’14 English–German description specifically tunes the normalization constant on newstest2015 and normalizes by |y|^α; the supplied passage gives no numerical α. The relevant wording is: “English-German we tune a length normalization constant on a separate development set (newstest2015)”. [S:f74f0352f640#44]
- **BLEU:** 1706.03762v7.pdf, p.8, Table 2 reports English–German scores of 27.3 for Transformer base and 28.4 for Transformer big: “Transformer (base model) 27.3 38.1” and “Transformer (big) 28.4 41.8”. [S:bee0d5905ca6#49] 1705.03122v3.pdf, p.6, Table 1 reports “ConvS2S (BPE 40K) 25.16” for English–German, with results averaged over several runs. [S:f74f0352f640#52] Its p.7 ensemble table reports “ConvS2S 26.43” and identifies the setting as “Accuracy of ensembles with eight models.” [S:f74f0352f640#55] The Transformer paper instead lists the ConvS2S ensemble at 26.36, so the two papers’ reported ensemble figures differ. [S:bee0d5905ca6#49] [S:f74f0352f640#55]

The comparison therefore does not hold beam width and length adjustment constant, preventing the BLEU difference alone from identifying the contribution of architecture. [S:bee0d5905ca6#53] [S:f74f0352f640#44] Moreover, “attention versus convolution” is an imprecise description: 1705.03122v3.pdf, p.2, explicitly says, “We also use attention in every decoder layer”. [S:f74f0352f640#9]

answer:
BERT uses next sentence prediction (NSP); RoBERTa removes it. BERT’s paper, 1810.04805v2.pdf, p.4, states: “we pre-train for a binarized next sentence prediction task”. [S:12a16f5a3e47#31] RoBERTa’s paper, 1907.11692v1.pdf, p.1, lists “removing the next sentence prediction objective” among its recipe changes. [S:e8aa84c227d7#4]

For masking, 1907.11692v1.pdf, p.4, reports that original BERT selected masks during preprocessing: “training data was duplicated 10 times so that each sequence is masked in 10 different ways over the 40 epochs of training.” [S:e8aa84c227d7#24] RoBERTa instead chooses masks whenever a sequence is presented: “we generate the masking pattern every time we feed a sequence to the model” (1907.11692v1.pdf, p.4). [S:e8aa84c227d7#24] The paper confirms its adoption: “we use dynamic masking in the remainder of the experiments” (p.4). [S:e8aa84c227d7#27]

Both retain masked language modeling (MLM): BERT explicitly names “the masked language model” (1810.04805v2.pdf, p.2), while RoBERTa describes retaining BERT’s pretraining approach with NSP removed and masking changed dynamically (1907.11692v1.pdf, p.10). [S:12a16f5a3e47#8] [S:e8aa84c227d7#66] The supplied RoBERTa passages support that retention through the described recipe changes, but do not explicitly state in one passage that its final objective is MLM alone.

citations.claim: The original BERT implementation selects masks during data preprocessing, with ten differently masked copies of each sequence.
citations.quote:
Speciﬁcally, we begin by training BERT models
with the same conﬁguration as BERTBASE (L =
12, H = 768, A = 12, 110M params).
4.1
Static vs. Dynamic Masking
As discussed in Section 2, BERT relies on ran-
domly masking and predicting tokens. The orig-
inal BERT implementation performed masking
once during data preprocessing, resulting in a sin-
gle static mask. To avoid using the same mask for
each training instance in every epoch, training data
was duplicated 10 times so that each sequence is
masked in 10 different ways over the 40 epochs of
training. Thus, each training sequence was seen
with the same mask four times during training.
We compare this strategy with dynamic mask-
ing where we generate the masking pattern every
time we feed a sequence to the model. This be-
comes crucial when pretraining for more steps or
with larger datasets.

answer:
Single BERT-Large reports 78.7 EM and 81.9 F1 on SQuAD 2.0 development data in its own paper, while single RoBERTa reports 86.5 EM and 89.4 F1: RoBERTa-minus-BERT differences are **+7.8 EM and +7.5 F1 percentage points**, calculated from those scores. [S:e06225395573#49] [S:7d01e285c820#58]

- **1810.04805v2.pdf, p. 7, Table 3:** “BERTLARGE (Single) 78.7 81.9 80.0 83.1”; the columns are “Dev Test EM F1 EM F1,” identifying the first two values as development scores. [S:e06225395573#49]
- **1907.11692v1.pdf, p. 9, Table 6:** “Single models on dev, w/o data augmentation” and “RoBERTa 88.9 94.6 86.5 89.4”; the columns are “SQuAD 1.1 SQuAD 2.0 EM F1 EM F1,” identifying 86.5/89.4 as the requested scores. [S:7d01e285c820#58]
- **Reporting discrepancy:** 1907.11692v1.pdf, p. 9, lists BERT-Large as 79.0 EM/81.8 F1, whereas 1810.04805v2.pdf, p. 7, reports 78.7/81.9; the differences above use each model’s own paper as requested. [S:7d01e285c820#58] [S:e06225395573#49]

**The numbers alone do not identify NSP removal as the cause:** 1907.11692v1.pdf, p. 1, describes several simultaneous modifications: “training the model longer, with bigger batches, over more data”; “removing the next sentence prediction objective”; “training on longer se- quences”; and “dynamically changing the mask- ing pattern applied to the training data.” [S:7d01e285c820#4] Its separate analysis on p. 5 says “removing the NSP loss matches or slightly improves downstream task performance,” but Table 2 explicitly concerns “base models pretrained over BOOKCORPUS and WIKIPEDIA,” so it does not establish that NSP removal caused the full single-model score differences above. [S:7d01e285c820#35] [S:7d01e285c820#30]

answer:
Original SQuAD contained exactly **107,785 question-answer pairs across 536 articles**; SQuAD 2.0 added exactly **53,775 new unanswerable questions** about the same paragraphs. The original count appears in 1606.05250v3.pdf, p. 2: “SQuAD contains 107,785 question-answer pairs on 536 articles”; the addition appears in 1806.03822v1.pdf, p. 2: “with 53,775 new, unanswerable questions about the same paragraphs.” [S:a536c47de57a#6] [S:9d83616f510f#9]

In 1606.05250v3.pdf, p. 2, the original collection consists of “questions posed by crowdworkers on a set of Wikipedia articles,” with each answer a “span, from the corresponding reading passage.” [S:a536c47de57a#6] In 1806.03822v1.pdf, p. 1, the follow-up explicitly combines existing SQuAD data with “unanswerable questions written adversarially by crowdworkers to look similar to answerable ones.” Thus, the original total and the new-question count measure different quantities. [S:9d83616f510f#1]

The follow-up specifies two challenging design properties in 1806.03822v1.pdf, p. 2: “(1) they are relevant to the paragraph, and (2) the paragraph contains a plausible answer—something of the same type as what the question asks for.” [S:9d83616f510f#9] Relevance prevents easy separation using superficial cues: p. 2 explains, “Otherwise, simple heuristics (e.g., based on word overlap) could distinguish answerable and unanswerable questions”. [S:9d83616f510f#11] Plausible answers act as distractors: p. 7 describes them as “distracting spans that could be mistaken for the correct answer.” [S:9d83616f510f#54]

citations.claim: SQuAD 2.0 combines existing SQuAD data with unanswerable questions written adversarially by crowdworkers to resemble answerable questions.
citations.quote:
Extractive reading comprehension sys-
tems can often locate the correct answer to
a question in a context document, but they
also tend to make unreliable guesses on
questions for which the correct answer is
not stated in the context. Existing datasets
either focus exclusively on answerable
questions, or use automatically generated
unanswerable questions that are easy to
identify. To address these weaknesses, we
present SQuAD 2.0, the latest version of
the Stanford Question Answering Dataset
(SQuAD). SQuAD 2.0 combines exist-
ing SQuAD data with over 50,000 unan-
swerable questions written adversarially
by crowdworkers to look similar to an-
swerable ones. To do well on SQuAD 2.0,
systems must not only answer questions
when possible, but also determine when no
answer is supported by the paragraph and
abstain from answering. SQuAD 2.0 is a
challenging natural language understand-
ing task

answer:
In the original SQuAD paper, Exact Match measures agreement with any reference answer, while token-overlap F1 measures overlap between predicted and reference answer tokens. [S:9ef61dedeed3#60] [S:9ef61dedeed3#61]

- **Exact Match and normalization — 1606.05250v3.pdf, p. 7:** Both metrics ignore punctuation and the articles “a,” “an,” and “the”; Exact Match is the percentage of predictions matching any ground-truth answer exactly: “Both metrics ignore punctuations and articles (a, an, the)” and “This metric measures the percent- age of predictions that match any one of the ground truth answers exactly.” [S:9ef61dedeed3#60]
- **Token-overlap F1 — 1606.05250v3.pdf, p. 7:** Predictions and references are treated as bags of tokens; the highest F1 across reference answers is selected for each question, then averaged across questions: “We treat the prediction and ground truth as bags of tokens, and compute their F1. We take the maximum F1 over all of the ground truth answers for a given question, and then average over all of the questions.” [S:9ef61dedeed3#61]
- **Unanswerable items — 1806.03822v1.pdf, p. 4:** Correct abstention scores 1 on both EM and F1; a nonempty answer scores 0 on both: “For negative examples, abstaining receives a score of 1, and any other response gets 0, for both exact match and F1.” [S:7cf0f3a73490#39]
- **Test threshold — 1806.03822v1.pdf, p. 4:** The threshold is chosen separately for each model on the development set to maximize development-set F1: “We tune this threshold separately for each model on the development set. When evaluating on the test set, we use the threshold that maximizes F1 score on the development set.” [S:7cf0f3a73490#38]

SQuAD 2.0 explicitly follows the original paper’s EM/F1 reporting and specifies the scoring rule for unanswerable examples. [S:7cf0f3a73490#39]

The original ResNet combines its identity shortcut and residual branch by addition, y = F(x, {Wi}) + x (1512.03385v1.pdf, p. 3: “y = F(x, {Wi}) + x.”), whereas DenseNet concatenates preceding features (1608.06993v5.pdf, p. 2: “we combine features by concatenating them.”). [S:1fcc885a5e28#21] [S:954c1b47e998#12]

In ResNet, addition is element-wise across corresponding channels (1512.03385v1.pdf, p. 3: “The element-wise addition is performed on two feature maps, channel by channel.”). [S:1fcc885a5e28#23] Within a DenseNet dense block, layer ℓ receives all preceding outputs, x₀ through xℓ₋₁, concatenated as its input (1608.06993v5.pdf, p. 3: “xℓ= Hℓ([x0, x1, . . . , xℓ−1])”). [S:954c1b47e998#26]

A direct architectural implication concerns feature dimensions: ResNet's unmodified identity shortcut requires matching input and output dimensions (1512.03385v1.pdf, p. 4: “The identity shortcuts (Eqn.(1)) can be directly used when the input and output are of the same dimensions”). [S:1fcc885a5e28#27] DenseNet instead accumulates features within its block, growing the available feature count by k per layer (1608.06993v5.pdf, p. 4: “Each layer adds k feature-maps of its own to this state.”). [S:954c1b47e998#35] The papers agree on the description of ResNet's combination operation: DenseNet explicitly describes the identity function and branch output as “combined by summation” (1608.06993v5.pdf, p. 3). [S:954c1b47e998#26]

ResNet reports **3.57% top-5 error** for its ILSVRC’15 ensemble on the ImageNet test set; DenseNet reports **6.34% single-crop / 5.54% 10-crop** for DenseNet-201 on the ImageNet validation set, so these results do not establish a like-for-like advantage. [S:50cf1f567758#53] [S:a03831a15e9d#48]

- **ResNet ensemble:** 1512.03385v1.pdf, p.7 states: “We combine six models of different depth to form an ensemble (only with two 152-layer ones at the time of submitting). This leads to 3.57% top-5 error on the test set (Table 5).” Its p.6 Table 5 specifies: “The top-5 error is on the test set of ImageNet and reported by the test server.” [S:50cf1f567758#62] [S:50cf1f567758#53]
- **ResNet evaluation:** 1512.03385v1.pdf, p.4 distinguishes comparison testing—“for comparison studies we adopt the standard 10-crop testing”—from its best-results protocol: “we adopt the fully- convolutional form as in [41, 13], and average the scores at multiple scales (images are resized such that the shorter side is in {224, 256, 384, 480, 640}).” The supplied evidence describes this best-results protocol but does not explicitly tie it to the particular six-model submission. [S:50cf1f567758#28] [S:50cf1f567758#29]
- **DenseNet-201:** 1608.06993v5.pdf, p.6 lists “DenseNet-201 22.58 / 21.46 6.34 / 5.54”; its caption identifies “top-1 and top-5 error rates on the ImageNet validation set, with single-crop / 10- crop testing.” [S:a03831a15e9d#48] The paper’s p.5 identifies ILSVRC 2012, with 50,000 validation images from 1,000 classes, and states: “apply a single-crop or 10-crop with size 224×224 at test time.” [S:a03831a15e9d#46] Its p.7 describes the model setup: “We simply replace the ResNet model with the DenseNet- BC network, and keep all the experiment settings exactly the same as those used for ResNet.” [S:a03831a15e9d#66]

**Comparison:** ResNet’s number is explicitly a six-model ensemble test result, whereas DenseNet’s table reports a named DenseNet-201 model’s validation results under crop-based evaluation; the supplied DenseNet evidence does not explicitly specify an ensemble size. These split and setup differences prevent these numbers alone from establishing a controlled head-to-head advantage. [S:50cf1f567758#62] [S:a03831a15e9d#48] [S:a03831a15e9d#66]

answer:
The original ViT paper reports **87.76% ± 0.03** ImageNet accuracy for JFT-pretrained ViT-L/16. [S:f6c924bc67fe#39]

In **2010.11929v2.pdf**, Table 2 (p.6) identifies the result as “Ours-JFT … (ViT-L/16)” and reports “87.76 ± 0.03”; its caption specifies that results are averaged over three fine-tuning runs. [S:f6c924bc67fe#39] The pretraining dataset is JFT-300M; the paper describes JFT as having “18k classes and 303M high-resolution images” and ImageNet, the downstream fine-tuning dataset, as “1k classes and 1.3M images” (p.4). [S:f6c924bc67fe#39] [S:f6c924bc67fe#28]

DeiT-B↑384 is the non-distilled model: p.8 explains that larger-resolution fine-tuning is denoted by “DeiT-B↑384,” whereas distillation is identified “with an alembic sign as DeiT⚗.” [S:cf900f68c20b#34] Its data regime is ImageNet-1k only: p.4 states “without requiring a large training dataset, i.e., with Imagenet1k only.” [S:cf900f68c20b#14]

The gap cannot be assigned to one design choice because these results change several factors together: the data regimes above, model capacity, operating resolution, and training procedure. [S:f6c924bc67fe#28] [S:cf900f68c20b#14] [S:f6c924bc67fe#30] [S:cf900f68c20b#34] [S:f6c924bc67fe#34] [S:cf900f68c20b#62]

- **Model configuration:** the ViT paper's p.5 table gives ViT-Large “24” layers, hidden size “1024,” and “307M” parameters, versus ViT-Base's “12” layers, “768” hidden size, and “86M” parameters. [S:f6c924bc67fe#30] The DeiT paper states on p.8 that DeiT-B “has the same architecture as ViT-B,” so this comparison uses different model sizes despite the shared architectural family. [S:cf900f68c20b#34] [S:f6c924bc67fe#30]
- **Resolution:** the ViT paper explicitly says on p.5, “For ImageNet results in Table 2, we ﬁne-tuned at higher resolution: 512 for ViT-L/16,” whereas the requested DeiT result operates at 384×384. [S:f6c924bc67fe#34] [S:cf900f68c20b#49]
- **Training procedure:** the ViT paper says on p.5, “For ﬁne-tuning we use SGD with momentum, batch size 512,” and specifies averaging “with a factor of 0.9999” for its Table 2 ImageNet results. [S:f6c924bc67fe#34] The DeiT paper's p.16 recipe lists AdamW, label smoothing 0.1, stochastic depth 0.1, repeated augmentation, Rand Augment, Mixup, Cutmix, and random erasing. [S:cf900f68c20b#62] Its p.15 caption describes “initial training at resolution 224×224” followed by “ﬁne-tuning at resolution 384×384.” [S:cf900f68c20b#59]

Thus, the reported accuracy difference compares complete training configurations; it does not isolate the effect of distillation, architecture, data scale, or any other individual ingredient. [S:f6c924bc67fe#39] [S:f6c924bc67fe#34] [S:cf900f68c20b#34] [S:cf900f68c20b#62]

At inference, each branch’s output embedding has its own linear classifier; late fusion adds the two classifiers’ softmax outputs to make the prediction. [S:95c24afe7977#33]
